plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 26: Biomolecules: Amino Acids, Peptides, and Proteins
plan.contextChunk: This figure pairs a titration curve for alanine with the structures present at each stage along it. The plot area is tinted pale blue and gridded; the vertical axis is labeled "pH" and runs from 0 to 12 with labeled ticks every 2 units, and the horizontal axis reads "Equivalents of HO-" and runs from 0.0 to 2.0 with ticks every 0.5. A magenta curve climbs from the bottom left in two legs, each a shallow buffering stretch followed by a steep rise, the two joined by a near-vertical jump at one equivalent. Three points on the curve are marked with an x and annotated: "pKa1 = 2.34" at 0.5 equivalent, "Isoelectric point = 6.01" at 1.0 equivalent, and "pKa2 = 9.69" at 1.5 equivalents. Thin arrows run from five positions on the curve out to bracketed structural formulas at the right, drawn with the ammonium nitrogen in magenta and the neutral amine nitrogen in blue: at the foot, the fully protonated cation with an intact carboxylic acid; at pKa1, a bracketed pair of that cation and the zwitterion; at the isoelectric point, the zwitterion alone; at pKa2, a bracketed pair of zwitterion and carboxylate anion; and at the top, the fully deprotonated anion. Aligning each structure with its own stretch of curve shows which species dominates over each pH range and pins down the pH at which the molecule carries no net charge.

demo_steps.title: Start fully protonated
demo_steps.narration: At very low equivalents of added base, alanine is mostly fully protonated: the amino group is H3N+ and the carboxyl group is COOH, giving a net positive charge.

demo_steps.title: First buffering point
demo_steps.narration: At 0.5 equivalents, the curve passes through pKa1 = 2.34. This is a 50:50 mixture of fully protonated alanine and the zwitterion, because the carboxyl proton is half removed.

demo_steps.title: Isoelectric zwitterion
demo_steps.narration: At 1.0 equivalent, alanine is mostly the zwitterion H3N+CH(CH3)COO−. The positive ammonium and negative carboxylate charges cancel, so the net charge is zero.

demo_steps.title: Second buffering point
demo_steps.narration: At 1.5 equivalents, the curve reaches pKa2 = 9.69. The zwitterion and fully deprotonated anion are present in equal amounts as the ammonium proton is half removed.

demo_steps.title: End fully deprotonated
demo_steps.narration: Near 2.0 equivalents, alanine is mostly H2NCH(CH3)COO−. Both acidic protons have been removed, leaving the molecule with a net negative charge.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The pKa points are half-conversion mixtures, while the isoelectric point is where the dominant alanine form has equal positive and negative internal charges and therefore zero net charge.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the figure as a wide layout with the titration plot on the left and alanine structures on the right connected by thin arrows. Use a pale blue gridded plotting area, black axes, and a bright magenta titration curve. The curve should rise gently near pH 2.34, steeply near one equivalent, flatten through the upper buffer region near pH 9.69, then rise again toward pH 12. Mark pKa1, the isoelectric point, and pKa2 with small x marks and leader annotations. The right panel should stack structures vertically from fully protonated at the bottom to fully deprotonated at the top; show bracketed pairs at the two pKa levels and single dominant species at the extremes and isoelectric point. Color protonated amino nitrogens magenta and neutral amino nitrogens blue. The slider marker should snap visually to the curve and update the highlighted arrow and structure region as it moves.

authoredContext:
Solving the two simultaneous equations gives [HA] = 0.83 and [A–] = 0.17. In other words, at pH = 9.00, 83% of alanine molecules in a 1.00 M solution are neutral (zwitterionic) and 17% are deprotonated. Similar calculations can be done at other pH values and the results plotted to give the titration curve shown in the figure.

Look carefully at the titration curve in the figure. In acid solution, the amino acid is protonated and exists primarily as a cation. In basic solution, the amino acid is deprotonated and exists primarily as an anion. In between the two is an intermediate pH at which the amino acid is exactly balanced between anionic and cationic forms, existing primarily as the neutral, dipolar zwitterion. This pH is called the amino acid’s isoelectric point (pI) and has a value of 6.01 for alanine.

Each leg of the titration curve is calculated separately. The first leg, from pH 1 to 6, corresponds to the dissociation of protonated alanine, H2A+. The second leg, from pH 6 to 11, corresponds to the dissociation of zwitterionic alanine, HA. It’s as if we started with H2A+ at low pH and then titrated with NaOH. When 0.5 equivalent of NaOH is added, the deprotonation of H2A+ is 50% complete; when 1.0 equivalent of NaOH is added, the deprotonation of H2A+ is finished and HA predominates; when 1.5 equivalents of NaOH is added, the deprotonation of HA is 50% complete; and when 2.0 equivalents of NaOH is added, the deprotonation of HA is finished.

A titration curve for alanine, plotted using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation. Each of the two legs is plotted separately. At pH < 1, alanine is entirely protonated; at pH = 2.34, alanine is a 50: 50 mix of protonated and neutral forms; at pH = 6.01, alanine is entirely neutral; at pH = 9.69, alanine is a 50: 50 mix of neutral and deprotonated forms; at pH > 11.5, alanine is entirely deprotonated.

The figure shows the titration curve for alanine. The x-axis represents equivalents of hydroxide ion and the y-axis represents the pH. It shows isoelectric point and two dissociation constant values.

demo_steps.narration: At 1.0 equivalent, alanine is mostly the zwitterion H3N+CH(CH3)COO−. The positive ammonium and negative carboxylate charges cancel, so the net charge is zero.

demo_steps.title: Second buffering point
demo_steps.narration: At 1.5 equivalents, the curve reaches pKa2 = 9.69. The zwitterion and fully deprotonated anion are present in equal amounts as the ammonium proton is half removed.

demo_steps.title: End fully deprotonated
demo_steps.narration: Near 2.0 equivalents, alanine is mostly H2NCH(CH3)COO−. Both acidic protons have been removed, leaving the molecule with a net negative charge.

plan.keyInsight: The pKa points are half-conversion mixtures, while the isoelectric point is where the dominant alanine form has equal positive and negative internal charges and therefore zero net charge.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the figure as a wide layout with the titration plot on the left and alanine structures on the right connected by thin arrows. Use a pale blue gridded plotting area, black axes, and a bright magenta titration curve. The curve should rise gently near pH 2.34, steeply near one equivalent, flatten through the upper buffer region near pH 9.69, then rise again toward pH 12. Mark pKa1, the isoelectric point, and pKa2 with small x marks and leader annotations. The right panel should stack structures vertically from fully protonated at the bottom to fully deprotonated at the top; show bracketed pairs at the two pKa levels and single dominant species at the extremes and isoelectric point. Color protonated amino nitrogens magenta and neutral amino nitrogens blue. The slider marker should snap visually to the curve and update the highlighted arrow and structure region as it moves.

discrepancies: The right-side alanine species panel is too compressed in the rendered view: the top fully deprotonated species and the pKa2 mixture are nearly on top of each other, unlike the well-separated molecular annotations in the source.

The chemical structures are much less clean than the source: several atom labels, subscripts, charges, and bond lines are crowded or misaligned, making the bracketed species hard to read at inline size.
The y-axis label 'pH' is effectively clipped/off-canvas in the screenshot, while it is clearly visible in the source figure.

Several leader arrows do not match the source styling and direction; the generated arrows visibly terminate at the molecular panels rather than reading as callouts from the curve landmarks to the corresponding species.
